lead: This unit is about running a software project and keeping its quality visible. You will learn to plan scope, measure work, estimate effort and cost, schedule tasks, manage risk, control changes, review work, maintain a live system and plan a release. After it, you can build a small project plan with numbers, a risk table and a release checklist.
about: This unit covers how a software project is planned, measured, estimated, scheduled, risk-checked, configured, reviewed, maintained and released. Chapter 6.1 sets the management view: people, product, process and project. Chapter 6.2 adds measurement, so plans use numbers. Chapter 6.3 turns size into effort and cost with COCOMO and decomposition. Chapter 6.4 places that effort on a calendar. Chapter 6.5 handles what can go wrong, and Chapter 6.6 controls changes to work products. Chapter 6.7 checks quality through assurance and reviews. Chapter 6.8 keeps a running system alive through maintenance and re-engineering. Chapter 6.9, taught by only a few universities, packages changes into releases.

chapters.idea: A software project is managed through four linked views: people, product, process and project, and these views become one practical plan.
chapters.depth: Cover the management spectrum: people, product, process and project. Cover the project planning process: scope, feasibility check, task list, estimate, schedule, risk plan and control. Some syllabi call this the four P's. Keep planning at one-page plan level.

figure.title: Four P's to plan
figure.aria: The four P's feed a project plan, which is executed, monitored and replanned.

chapters.example: A college team of 6 students has 10 weeks and ₹40,000 to build a hostel mess app with 8 must-have features. Write the four P's and give one control point for each. Answer: People: 1 Android developer, 1 tester, 1 designer. Product: 8 features, first release keeps 5. Process: weekly build, review at week 5. Project: spend check at week 6 and week 10.
chapters.trap: Skipping product scope and starting with a schedule. The four P's are views of one project, not four phases.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: process models and reasons projects fail.
chapters.leave: Detailed WBS and Gantt to 6.4; COCOMO to 6.3; risk table to 6.5; process models to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Measurement turns a plan into numbers that show whether process and product are improving.
chapters.depth: Cover measurement principles; measure, metric and indicator; process metrics, project metrics and product metrics; size, effort, defect and schedule metrics; metrics for software quality: correctness, reliability, maintainability and usability; leading and lagging indicators; goal-question-metric idea.

figure.aria: Software measurement splits into process, project and product metrics, each with one example.

chapters.example: A team planned 200 person-days and used 230. Review found 120 defects; after release users found 30. Compute effort variance and defect removal efficiency. Answer: effort variance = (230 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100% = 15% over plan. DRE = 120 ÷ (120 + 30) × 100% = 80%.
chapters.trap: Using a product metric as a process metric. DRE uses all defects, not only the defects found in review.
chapters.leave: Test metrics and test reporting to Unit 5; detailed function point counting to 6.3.

chapters.idea: Size can be converted into effort, duration and cost by decomposition and by an empirical model such as COCOMO.
chapters.depth: Cover decomposition: software sizing with LOC and function points; problem-based and process-based estimation; use-case estimation; reconciliation. Cover basic COCOMO: E = a × (KLOC)^b and D = c × E^d, where E is effort in person-months, KLOC is thousands of delivered source lines, D is duration in months, and a, b, c, d are mode constants. Organic: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38. Semidetached and embedded use different constants. Cost = E × rate. Mention that intermediate COCOMO adds cost drivers.

figure.aria: Effort rises faster than size; the marked point is 10 KLOC at about 26.9 person-months.

chapters.example: An organic project is 10 KLOC. Use basic COCOMO to find effort, duration and average staff. Rate is ₹80,000 per person-month. Find cost. Answer: E = 2.4 × 10^1.05 ≈ 26.9 person-months. D = 2.5 × 26.9^0.38 ≈ 8.7 months. Average staff ≈ 26.9 ÷ 8.7 ≈ 3.1 people. Cost ≈ 26.9 × ₹80,000 ≈ ₹21.5 lakh.
chapters.trap: Putting lines into COCOMO instead of KLOC. A person-month is effort, not one calendar month.
chapters.leave: Scheduling and resource leveling to 6.4; risk to 6.5.

chapters.idea: A schedule turns effort into dated tasks and shows the critical path that controls the finish date.
chapters.depth: Cover WBS, task dependencies, effort and duration, Gantt charts, PERT/CPM, critical path, slack, schedule tracking and timeboxing. Some syllabi call this scheduling and tracking.

figure.aria: Tasks A, B, D, F form the 14-day critical path; C and E have slack.

chapters.example: Tasks: A takes 3 days; B takes 4 days after A; C takes 2 days after A; D takes 5 days after B; E takes 3 days after C; F takes 2 days after D and E. Find the critical path, project duration and slack of C and E. Answer: A-B-D-F = 3 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 14 days. C and E each have 4 days of slack.
chapters.trap: Choosing the path with the most tasks. The critical path is the longest path by duration, not by count.
chapters.leave: Cost estimation to 6.3; earned-value management to advanced project management outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Risks are identified early, ranked by probability and impact, and handled with a written RMMM plan.
chapters.depth: Cover reactive versus proactive strategies; software risks; risk identification: product, process and technology; risk projection: probability, impact and risk exposure; risk refinement; risk table; RMMM: mitigation, monitoring and management; RMMM plan contents. Some syllabi call management contingency.

figure.aria: Risk work moves from identification to projection, refinement, the RMMM plan, monitoring and management.

chapters.example: R1 key developer leaves: probability 0.2, impact 6 person-weeks. R2 payment API changes: probability 0.4, impact 3 person-weeks. R3 server outage: probability 0.1, impact 10 person-weeks. Compute risk exposure, rank the risks, and write one RMMM action for the top risk. Answer: R1 = 0.2 × 6 = 1.2; R2 = 0.4 × 3 = 1.2; R3 = 0.1 × 10 = 1.0. R1 and R2 tie at the top. For R1, use pair programming and a written handover note; monitor monthly; keep a backup developer ready.
chapters.trap: Using probability as a percentage such as 20 instead of 0.2. Risk exposure = probability × impact.
chapters.leave: Change control mechanics to 6.6; testing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Configuration management keeps every work product under version control and every change approved against a baseline.
chapters.depth: Cover SCM: configuration items, baseline, change request, change control board, status accounting and configuration audit; version control; build and release records; SCM in CI/CD.

figure.title: Change to baseline
figure.aria: A change request is analysed, approved by the change control board, becomes a new baseline, and then moves to build or release.

chapters.example: Baseline B1 has code login 1.0, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.0. CR-07 changes login to 1.1 and test plan to 1.1. Write B2 and say which items changed. Answer: B2 has login 1.1, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.1. Two items changed.
chapters.trap: Treating version control as the whole of SCM. SCM also covers change control, status accounting and audits.
chapters.leave: CI/CD pipeline tools to Unit 5; detailed Ansible playbooks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Software quality assurance builds quality into the process, and technical reviews catch defects before testing.
chapters.depth: Cover the SQA process and standards; technical reviews: informal review, walkthrough and inspection; roles: moderator, author, reviewer and recorder; review checklist; defect logging; SQA versus QC.

figure.title: Review flow
figure.aria: A formal review moves from planning and overview to preparation, inspection, rework and follow-up.

chapters.example: A 4,000-line module is reviewed for 20 hours. The team finds 20 defects. Testing later finds 4 more. Compute review rate, defect density after all defects, and review effectiveness. Answer: review rate = 4,000 ÷ 20 = 200 lines per hour. Defect density = 24 ÷ 4 KLOC = 6 defects per KLOC. Review effectiveness = 20 ÷ (20 + 4) × 100% = 83.3%.
chapters.trap: Equating SQA with testing. An inspection is formal and has defined roles; a walkthrough is less formal.
chapters.leave: White-box and black-box test design to Unit 4; test automation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Maintenance keeps a live system useful, and re-engineering rebuilds an ageing system when patching costs too much.
chapters.depth: Cover maintenance types: corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive; maintenance cost; reverse engineering; restructuring; re-engineering; legacy systems; maintenance process and impact analysis.

figure.title: Re-engineering path
figure.aria: Legacy code is reverse engineered, restructured and re-engineered into a new system.

chapters.example: A payroll system gets 500 change requests a year; each costs 8 hours. Re-engineering costs 3,000 hours and is expected to cut requests to 100 a year. Compute yearly saving and payback. Answer: saving = (500 − 100) × 8 = 3,200 hours per year. Payback = 3,000 ÷ 3,200 = 0.94 years, about 11 months.
chapters.trap: Calling every change corrective maintenance. Maintenance also adapts to new platforms and improves future work.
chapters.leave: Regression testing details to Unit 4; deployment automation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A release is a controlled, versioned package of changes that moves from staging to production with a rollback plan.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover release scope, semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, release candidate, release checklist, staging to production, rollback, release notes and feature flags. Keep to one release cycle.

figure.title: Release gate
figure.aria: A release moves from feature freeze to release candidate, sign-off, production, monitoring and possible rollback.

chapters.example: Current release is 2.4.1. Next release adds a backward-compatible feature; then a bug fix; then a breaking API change. Give the three version numbers under semantic versioning. Answer: 2.5.0, then 2.5.1, then 3.0.0.
chapters.trap: Calling every build a release. A version number must signal compatibility, not just count commits.
chapters.leave: Deployment pipelines to Unit 5; full SCM detail to 6.6.
